sentences: I was born in nineteen fifty-two in Thrissur, in Kerala, in a house my grandfather had built.
It had a tiled roof of red clay, and in the monsoon the rain poured off the eaves in silver ropes.
In the middle of the house was an open courtyard with a tulsi plant on a small stone platform.
My mother watered it every morning before she lit the lamp, and I never saw her miss a day.
My father was a schoolmaster, so the house was always full of exercise books waiting to be marked.
He sat on the long wooden verandah in the evenings with a red pencil behind his ear.
I have two sisters, Radha who was older and Meena who was younger, and we shared one big room.
We slept on woven mats, and the floor was cool red oxide that my mother polished every week.
The kitchen was at the back, with a clay hearth and a row of brass vessels that gleamed like small suns.
My grandmother ground rice batter on a heavy stone.
I can still hear the sound of it.
Even as a boy I wanted to know how things worked.
So I studied the house like a machine.
I noticed that the courtyard let hot air rise and pulled cool air through all the rooms.
The roof beams were jackwood, and my father said they would outlast all of us.
There was a well behind the kitchen.
I loved to lower the bucket and count the seconds until the splash.
Beside the well grew a mango tree that my grandfather had planted the year he finished the house.
Our neighbour on the left was a carpenter named Kunjan, and I spent hours watching him work.
He cut his joints without a single nail, and he let me hold the chisel when nobody was looking.
On the right lived a widow who kept hens, and her cockerel woke the whole lane before dawn.
The lane itself was red mud, which turned into a slippery river whenever the rains came.
We walked to school barefoot with our books wrapped in banana leaf against the wet.
In the evenings my father read aloud to us from old almanacs and sometimes from the Ramayana.
My sisters and I sat on the verandah steps, and the oil lamp threw our shadows against the pillars.
When electricity finally reached our lane, I was about eight years old.
I remember the first bulb, a yellow thing hanging on a twisted wire in the courtyard.
The whole street came to look at it, and my father switched it on with great ceremony.
I asked him where the light came from.
He said from a power station far away.
That answer did not satisfy me at all, and I think it started the engineer in me.
I badly wanted to see the wire that carried it and follow it all the way back.
Food in that house was simple, rice and fish curry cooked with kokum and a little coconut oil.
My mother cooked the fish in a clay pot, and she said clay held the flavour better than metal.
On festival days the courtyard was drawn over with rice flour patterns.
Relatives arrived from distant villages and slept wherever there was a space on the floor.
The house seemed to expand for them, and nobody was ever turned away.
When I think of that place now, I feel the cool floor under my feet first.
After that I smell wet earth and woodsmoke, and then I hear my mother calling us in for rice.
It was a modest house, but it taught me that a good building breathes.
I carried that idea with me for the rest of my life.
My closest friend as a boy was Gopalan, whom everybody called Gopi, and he lived three houses down our lane.
His father repaired bicycles in a tiny shed at the corner, and the shed smelled of rubber and oil.
Gopi could mend a punctured tube faster than any grown man.
He was only nine.
I admired that more than I admired anything my schoolbooks taught me.
We were quite different.
He was loud and quick while I was quiet and careful.
Somehow the two of us fitted together like a nut and a bolt.
In the afternoons we sat in the shed, and he showed me how a freewheel clicked and why a chain needed oil.
I would take the little ratchet apart on a newspaper and put it back together, spring by spring.
Gopi's father pretended not to notice, although he always left the smallest spanner within my reach.
Our great project, in the summer I turned eleven, was a water wheel in the stream behind the paddy fields.
We cut the paddles from coconut husk and fixed them to a hub made from an old bicycle wheel.
For three days it refused to turn, and Gopi wanted to give up and go fishing.
I insisted that the paddles were too shallow, so we deepened them with a borrowed knife.
Then the wheel began to turn, slowly at first, and we both shouted until the egrets flew off.
We had no idea what to do with it, so we simply sat on the bank and watched it spin.
That was enough for us, and it remains one of the happiest afternoons of my childhood.
Gopi was not a good student, and the teachers often rapped his knuckles with a ruler.
I tried to help him with arithmetic, but he learned better with his hands than with numbers.
When I wrote out a sum, he would shake his head and ask me to show him with pebbles.
So we spread pebbles on the verandah floor and added them up in heaps.
His mother brought us sweet banana fritters while we worked, and she called me the little professor.
When we were thirteen, Gopi left school to work full time with his father.
I felt his absence in the classroom like a missing tooth.
Still, we met every Sunday at the stream, and he told me about the bicycles of the whole district.
He knew which families had Raleighs, which had Hercules machines, and who rode too heavily on the pedals.
When I went away to the engineering college, he gave me a small brass bell for my bicycle.
I kept that bell on my desk for years, even after I no longer owned a bicycle.
Later he expanded the shed into a proper shop with three mechanics and a signboard in red paint.
I visited him whenever I returned to Kerala, and we always drank tea on the same wooden bench.
He had grown stout and grey, and he laughed exactly as he had at nine years old.
We talked about the wheel in the stream more than anything else.
He once told me that he still looked at running water and thought of our paddles.
I confess that I do the same, even in a desert country where water is precious.
Gopi died a few years ago, and his son sent me a photograph of the shop with the old bench.
I have it framed beside my chessboard now.
Some friendships are made of long conversations, but ours was made of tools and small repairs.
I think that is why it lasted so well.
Whenever something breaks in my house, I hear his voice telling me to be patient.
He taught me that most machines forgive you if you are gentle and curious.
My school was a long low building of whitewashed brick, about a mile from our house.
We called it the Board School, and it stood beside a banyan tree that older boys were forbidden to climb.
Every morning we sat on benches in rows, and the headmaster walked down the aisle with his hands behind his back.
His name was Mister Pillai, and he had a voice like a slow drum.
We began each day with a prayer and then recited the multiplication tables up to twenty.
I can still repeat them in the same singsong rhythm, and sometimes they help me fall asleep.
We wrote on slates until the fifth class.
The chalk dust settled on our fingers like flour.
When we finally received notebooks, I treated mine as if it were made of gold leaf.
My handwriting was neat because my father had trained me to hold the pen lightly.
Mathematics was my favourite subject, and I loved geometry above all the other branches.
I liked the idea that a drawing could prove something, that a circle and a ruler could settle an argument.
Our geometry teacher was a thin man with a limp, and he drew perfect circles freehand on the blackboard.
Once I asked him how he managed it, and he said that he simply stopped worrying.
I thought about that sentence for years, and I now think it was good advice for engineers.
Our English lessons were taught from a worn reader printed in London, full of snowy villages.
We had never seen snow, so we imagined it as a kind of cold white rice.
Still, I enjoyed the stories, and I read them aloud to my sister Meena at night.
Science classes were held on Fridays, and the teacher brought a magnet and a glass jar of mercury.
He let us watch the silver drops roll across a tray, and nobody dared to breathe.
I was lucky to have a father who was himself a teacher, though he worked at another school across the river.
He never helped me in class and never boasted about my marks.
Instead he corrected my spelling at home, patiently, with his red pencil.
At the end of the year there was a prize day in the courtyard, with plastic chairs and a rented microphone.
I received the prize for mathematics three times.
Each time my mother wrapped the book in brown paper.
The other boys did not hold it against me, because I let them copy my homework on the way to school.
In the monsoon the classrooms leaked.
We moved our benches into the dry corners.
The teachers carried on as if nothing was happening, and a puddle on the floor was just part of the lesson.
Lunch was a steel tin of rice and pickle, and we ate sitting under the banyan tree.
There was a boy named Thomas who brought dried fish, and the smell sent the crows into a frenzy.
We played a game with tamarind seeds during the break, and I was surprisingly good at it.
Discipline in those days was strict, and the cane was kept in the headmaster's cupboard.
I was caned only once, for laughing during an inspection, and I considered it an unfair price.
Our exams were conducted in a hall that smelled of sandalwood and old paper.
I sat very straight, because I believed that good posture helped the brain.
When the results came, they were pinned on a board outside.
We all crowded around it.
My name stood near the top, and I felt a quiet joy that I have rarely felt since.
Looking back, I am grateful for those plain rooms and simple tools.
They taught me discipline and the pleasure of a correct answer.
My first real job was at a pump manufacturing works in Coimbatore, in nineteen seventy-five.
I was twenty-three years old, with a freshly printed degree and a very serious moustache.
The works made centrifugal pumps for farmers, and the main shed echoed like a cathedral full of hammers.
My title was junior design engineer, which meant that I did whatever the seniors preferred not to do.
On my first morning the chief draughtsman handed me a pencil and a pile of worn drawings.
He told me to check every dimension against a sample casting on the bench.
I measured with a vernier caliper, and I found a mistake in the very first drawing.
The shaft diameter was off by two tenths of a millimetre, and the casting had been poured wrongly for years.
He looked at me for a long moment and then said that I might stay.
I lived in a rented room above a tea shop, ten minutes by foot from the gate.
The landlady was a retired nurse who served me idli every morning and charged very little.
Mister Raghavan, the owner, walked the shed every morning at seven.
He knew every worker by name and asked after their children.
My salary was four hundred and fifty rupees a month, and I sent a quarter of it home.
On Sundays the whole compound was silent, and I enjoyed that stillness.
My mother wrote to ask whether I was eating enough.
Each evening I walked back past the lathe shop and watched the apprentices sweep up the bright metal curls.
I learned more from those men than from many professors, because they had skills in their fingertips.
A foreman named Subramaniam taught me how to listen to a bearing and hear when it was tired.
He held a long steel rod against the housing and pressed the other end to his ear.
I tried it dozens of times before I could hear the faint grinding he described.
Eventually I did hear it, and he clapped me on the shoulder as though I had passed a great examination.
We built a test rig for the pumps, with a glass tank and a row of pressure gauges.
I was put in charge of it, and I took the role extremely seriously.
Every pump that left the works carried my initials on a small tag, which made me prouder than a medal.
There was one difficult customer, a landowner from Palakkad who returned a pump three times.
Each time I travelled to his farm and found nothing wrong except that his well had dropped.
Finally I explained the water level to him with a diagram drawn in the dust.
He laughed, paid for a longer suction pipe, and sent me home with a sack of jaggery.
Life in Coimbatore was quiet, and my entertainment was a weekly cricket match on a dusty ground.
We played with a taped tennis ball, and I bowled slow spin that confused no one.
After the match we drank sweet tea from glasses at a roadside stall.
The works taught me patience and the dignity of ordinary machines.
I also discovered that a well made thing gives its maker a private satisfaction.
After three years I began to feel restless, as if the shed had become too small.
A senior colleague mentioned that engineers were wanted in the Gulf, where the coastal plants needed careful hands.
I wrote a letter that evening, in my neat schoolmaster's handwriting, and posted it the next morning.
Six months later an answer came, and my whole life turned on that single envelope.
I will always be grateful to the old pump works for giving me my footing.
Even now, when I hear a pump humming in a building, I stop to listen.
The biggest move of my life was in nineteen seventy-nine, when I flew from Kochi to Abu Dhabi.
I was twenty-seven, and I had never been on an aeroplane before.
My mother packed a tin of banana chips and a small bottle of coconut oil in my bag.
At the airport my father held my hand a little too long, and said nothing at all.
The flight was long, and I pressed my forehead to the window whenever the lights of a town went by.
When the door opened at Abu Dhabi, the heat struck me like the opening of a furnace.
It was August, and the air was so humid that my spectacles fogged instantly.
A driver from the company met me with a card that spelled my name wrongly.
We drove along a road that was almost empty, with sand on either side and the sea shining ahead.
I remember that the city was small then, with low white buildings and a great many cranes.
The company gave me a room in a shared house near the plant, with four other bachelors.
We had one refrigerator, one television, and a rule that nobody cooked fish on weekdays.
My roommates were from Kerala, Punjab, and Sri Lanka, and we ate together in the evenings.
I learned to make dal and chapati from a Punjabi engineer named Harbans, who treated cooking as a science.
Harbans kept a jar of green chillies on the windowsill and guarded it jealously.
The plant itself stood on the coast, and its job was to turn seawater into drinking water.
I found that astonishing, because I had grown up with so much rain that I never thought about thirst.
Here every drop was counted, and nobody wasted a glass.
The first months were lonely, and I wrote a letter home every Sunday on thin blue paper.
Letters took ten days each way, and I read the replies until the folds went soft.
My mother wrote about the mango tree, and my father wrote about the school.
Sometimes I stood at the window at night and tried to imagine the courtyard and the tulsi plant.
Slowly the city welcomed me, because the people were generous and the shopkeepers were patient.
A Lebanese baker near our house gave me warm bread every morning and refused to take money on Fridays.
On my first payday I bought a small radio and tuned it to Malayalam songs.
The shortwave signal came and went, but I loved it.
That little radio sat on my shelf for twenty years.
I learned a few words of Arabic, enough to bargain and to thank people.
On weekends we drove to the corniche, and the sea breeze felt like a cool hand on the forehead.
After two years, my family arranged my marriage, and Lakshmi came to join me in a small flat.
She found the first winter harder than I had, because she missed her sisters.
We bought a small stove and a pressure cooker, and the flat began to smell like home.
Our sons were born in that country, Arun first and then Vivek, and they grew up with two homes.
I never planned to stay for my entire career, and yet I did.
Each year I told myself that I would return to Kerala, and each year the plant needed me.
Moving was hard, but it widened me, and I do not regret it.
A person can plant roots in two places if he waters both carefully.
Now my sons say that Abu Dhabi is their home, and I understand them perfectly.
When I visit Thrissur, people call me the Gulf man, and I smile.
I am a man of two courtyards, one of red clay and one of white stone.
One journey I have never forgotten is the overnight train to Madras, when I was seventeen.
I had been called to an interview for a seat at the engineering college there.
My father bought me a second class ticket, and my mother packed lemon rice in a banana leaf.
It was the first time I had travelled so far alone, and I felt very grown up.
The carriage was crowded, with families on every bench and baskets stacked in the aisle.
A ceiling fan turned lazily, and the wooden seats were polished by many years of travellers.
The ticket collector punched my ticket with a small steel tool and wished me luck.
Because the night was warm, I sat near the open door to catch the breeze.
I had taken off my shoes and tucked them beside me, which was a terrible mistake.
At some dark station the train lurched, my elbow knocked them, and my only pair of shoes fell out of the carriage door.
I watched them tumble onto the track, and I could do nothing but stare.
A kind old man nearby told me that the shoes had gone to a better place.
I did not laugh, and I spent the night wondering what I would wear.
Rain began after midnight, and the smell of wet earth came through the door.
The wheels beat a steady rhythm that I tried to count against my pulse.
By morning the sky was pink over the roofs of the city.
At dawn in Madras a porter lent me a pair of rubber sandals that were two sizes too large.
I flapped to the interview like a duck, and the panel looked at my feet with open amusement.
I did not get the seat, but I did earn a few smiles.
Apart from the shoes, the journey was a long lesson in how the country looked.
The train ran through paddy fields shining with water, and later through dry red country dotted with palmyra trees.
At every halt vendors rushed along the platform with tea, boiled eggs, and sweet crisp murukku.
I leaned out of the window and listened to their cries, which rose and fell like a kind of music.
At Palakkad the engine was changed, and I watched men uncouple it with enormous iron hooks.
That was my first look at heavy machinery doing something with great calm precision.
I memorised how the coupling worked, and I drew it in my notebook between two lines of arithmetic.
A girl of about ten sat opposite me, and she shared her tamarind sweets without saying a word.
Her mother told me that they were travelling to see a grandfather who was very ill.
I said a small prayer for him, and the girl solemnly nodded.
When she got down at a small station, she waved with both hands until I could no longer see her.
I still wonder what happened to that family and that grandfather.
After the interview I walked to the beach and sat on the sand in my enormous sandals.
It was my first view of a true ocean, and it was larger than any water I could imagine.
The waves arrived in long grey lines and fell over themselves with a sound like distant trains.
I felt tiny and, strangely, quite happy.
The return journey was calmer, and a conductor found me a pair of canvas shoes at a station stall.
When I came home, my sisters laughed for a week about the sandals.
My father said that a man learns more from a lost shoe than from a found coin.
I never took my shoes off near an open door again.
In a sense that journey began my travelling life, though I did not know it then.
A celebration I remember especially well is my own wedding, in nineteen eighty-one.
I had come home from Abu Dhabi for one month, and the whole family had been planning for a year.
The wedding took place at a temple near Guruvayur, in the cool early morning.
Lakshmi wore a cream and gold sari, and she kept her eyes lowered until the very last ritual.
Her father tied the sacred thread with hands that trembled slightly.
The priest chanted in a low voice, and the smell of camphor drifted around us.
I wore a white mundu and a silk shawl, and I was so nervous that my hands shook.
My father arranged everything, from the priest to the flowers, with the care of a man marking an examination.
The pandal was built from bamboo and coconut fronds, and it smelled wonderfully of green leaves.
The cooks arrived at four in the morning to light the great wood fires.
The bride's family had decorated the entrance with fresh jasmine strings.
Over three hundred guests came, and the banana leaves were laid out in long rows on the floor.
A photographer from Thrissur set up a tripod and made everyone stand still.
The children were given small sweets, and they hid the wrappers in their pockets.
My aunt pressed a coin into my hand for luck.
The feast began with a pinch of salt and a spoonful of plain rice, and then came the endless dishes.
There was sambar, avial, olan, a sweet pumpkin curry, three kinds of pickle, and crisp banana chips.
The payasam arrived at the end in great brass vessels, and the cooks ladled it out with long spoons.
I believe I told you about my shoes and the Madras train last time.
At the temple door I had to leave my shoes outside, and my cousins, who knew the old story, laughed at me.
One of them even stood guard over my footwear for the whole ceremony.
Back to the feast, my mother and her sisters had cooked for two days without sleeping.
My uncle Raman insisted on carrying the pickle jar himself, because he did not trust the servers.
There was a small band with a clarinet and drums, and they played film songs from the nineteen sixties.
My sister Radha danced with her friends, and Meena sang a verse from a Carnatic composition.
Her voice was clear and true, and the elders went quiet to listen.
I was very moved, because I knew that she had practised for weeks in secret.
Lakshmi and I walked around the sacred fire seven times, and each round felt like a promise.
Her bangles rang softly, and I could hear them above the music.
In the afternoon the rain came suddenly, and everyone ran under the pandal laughing.
The water dripped through the fronds, and the children stamped in the puddles.
I remember thinking that the rain had come to bless us, just as it blessed our house in my childhood.
By evening the guests had left, and a tired quiet settled over the courtyard.
Lakshmi and I sat on the verandah, and she asked me whether I was happy.
I said that I was happier than I could measure, which for an engineer is a great confession.
She laughed, and I knew then that I had married someone who understood me.
Our photographs from that day have faded to brown, but my memory of it is still in colour.
We celebrated our fortieth anniversary with a small dinner, and my sons made a toast.
They asked for the old story of the wedding feast, and I told it again.
I think a good celebration is one that you can taste years afterwards.
In my working life, a typical day began at five in the morning, before the sun was properly up.
Lakshmi made me strong tea with cardamom.
I drank it standing at the kitchen window.
By six I was in my car, driving the empty road toward the plant on the coast.
The plant was a cluster of steel towers, pipes, and tanks that hummed all day and all night.
Its purpose was to boil seawater and capture the steam, which condensed into fresh water.
Every morning I began with a walk through the whole facility, notebook in hand.
I checked the pressure gauges one by one.
I wrote the readings in the same blue ink.
I trusted that notebook more than any computer, because it never crashed and I could smell its pages.
The heat in the plant was fierce, so we wore light cotton shirts and kept a bottle of water in every pocket.
Near the brine pumps there was a constant roar, and we talked with our hands.
The operators on the night shift would meet me at the control room with a short report.
They were Indian, Pakistani, Egyptian, and Filipino men, and we shared a respect for good order.
At seven thirty I sat down with the shift supervisor, and we discussed any odd sounds or smells.
A smell can tell you something is wrong long before a sensor does.
After that I looked at the maintenance list, and I planned which valves or filters needed attention.
Scale was our eternal enemy, because the minerals in seawater coated the tubes like a stubborn crust.
So we dosed the water with chemicals and cleaned the tubes every few months.
At ten the managers arrived, and we held a short meeting around a long table with weak coffee.
I disliked long meetings, so I kept mine to exactly twenty minutes by my wristwatch.
Midday was the hardest time, when the sun on the steel made the whole place shimmer.
I often ate lunch at my desk.
It was a steel tin of rice and fish curry that Lakshmi had packed.
The younger engineers teased me about it, and then they begged for a taste.
In the afternoon I wrote reports, with a pencil first and then a typewriter, and later a keyboard.
Every report ended with a section called recommendations, which I considered the heart of the matter.
At four I went out for a second round, and the light turned golden on the pipes.
That was my favourite hour, when the machines seemed calm and almost friendly.
Before leaving, I would sign the logbook and hand over to the evening engineer.
The drive home was slow, with the sea on my left and the sky changing colours.
At home my sons would be doing homework on the dining table.
They would show me their sums.
Dinner was at eight, and Lakshmi insisted that we all ate together without the television.
After dinner I played a game of chess with Arun, who took a long time over each move.
Then I read the newspaper from the back page to the front, which is how a cricket lover does it.
By ten I was asleep, and the next day would repeat in almost the same way.
Some people might call such a life dull, but I found a deep satisfaction in its rhythm.
A plant is like a body, and a good engineer learns to take its pulse every morning.
I kept that routine for thirty-five years, and I would happily keep it again.
The person who influenced me most, after my parents, was a chief engineer named Mister Duncan Hale.
He was a Scotsman with white eyebrows and a voice like gravel in a bucket.
I met him in nineteen eighty-three, when I had been in Abu Dhabi for four years.
He had worked on coastal plants in three continents, and he spoke of them as old friends.
On my first day under him, he walked me around the plant without saying a word for an hour.
At the end he asked me what I had noticed, and I gave a long technical answer.
He shook his head and said that I had looked at the machines but not at the men.
I did not understand at first, and I felt a little stung.
Later I saw what he meant, because the operators knew things that no drawing contained.
One of them could tell by the pitch of a pump when a seal was about to fail.
Mister Hale made me sit with those men for a week and simply listen.
It was the best week of training I ever had.
He taught me to keep a logbook with complete honesty, including my own mistakes.
He said that an engineer who hides an error is building a bridge with a missing bolt.
I wrote my first mistake in the book soon after, a valve that I had left half open.
He read the entry, gave me a nod, and never mentioned it again.
In the evenings he would invite a few of us to his flat for tea and shortbread.
He kept a shelf of old technical books, and he let us borrow them freely.
He also played the bagpipes badly, which we all politely pretended to admire.
He kept a small tin of peppermints on his desk and offered one to every visitor.
He believed that every plant had a personality, and he named the pumps after Scottish rivers.
Our largest pump was called the Spey, and it never failed him.
The operators loved that habit, and soon they were naming the valves too.
I was amused to discover that he loved Carnatic music, which a colleague had played for him once.
He asked me to bring him recordings, and I brought him a tape of a veena recital.
On Fridays he lectured us for ten minutes on the history of water.
He listened with his eyes closed and said that the music reminded him of well tuned machinery.
I thought it was the nicest compliment a Scotsman could give.
When a new contract required long nights, he worked right beside us, with his sleeves rolled up.
He never raised his voice, and he never took credit for our ideas.
When I was promoted to supervisor, he gave me a brass slide rule that had belonged to his own teacher.
I still keep it in a drawer, wrapped in a soft cloth.
He retired in nineteen ninety and went back to a small town near Aberdeen.
We wrote to each other at Christmas for twenty years, and his letters were always short.
The last one said only that the heather was in bloom and that he missed the heat.
I felt a deep sadness when his daughter wrote to tell me that he had died.
I try to treat my own juniors in the way that he treated me.
I listen first, I give them real responsibility, and I let them make small mistakes.
A good mentor is someone who makes you slightly better than you believed you could be.
He did that for me, and I am grateful every time I open that drawer.
One thing I am especially proud of happened in the summer of nineteen ninety-eight.
That year the heat was terrible, and the demand for water in Abu Dhabi had never been higher.
Our plant was running at full capacity, and the margin for error had almost disappeared.
Then one of the main circulation pumps began to shake, and the vibration grew worse each hour.
The manufacturer sent a message saying that a replacement would take six weeks to arrive.
We did not have six weeks, because the city could not do without that water.
I gathered the best operators and mechanics in the control room, and we spread the drawings on the table.
Everyone looked tired, and nobody offered an idea for a long minute.
Then I remembered my days at the pump works in Coimbatore and Subramaniam with his steel rod.
I asked a mechanic to press the rod against the housing and listen to the bearing.
He heard a harsh grinding, and we knew the fault was in the bearing, not in the impeller.
That was a smaller problem than we had feared, and it could be solved on site.
We needed a certain kind of ceramic bearing, which we did not have in the store.
A young engineer named Faisal suggested that a neighbouring plant might have a spare.
I telephoned their chief and explained our difficulty, and he agreed to lend it that same night.
Faisal drove two hours through the dark with the bearing wrapped in a towel on the seat.
We worked until sunrise, with the pump opened up like a patient on a table.
Lakshmi had packed flasks of tea and a box of sweet biscuits for the crew.
We drank it sitting on upturned crates, too tired to speak.
I fitted the bearing myself, and I tightened the bolts in the sequence that Mister Hale had taught me.
When we restarted the pump, it ran so smoothly that the operators cheered.
Outside, the sky was turning from black to a pale grey.
Faisal fell asleep on the bench with grease on his cheek.
The vibration gauge showed almost nothing, and I wrote the number in my notebook with trembling fingers.
We had lost only nine hours of capacity, and the city never noticed.
Nobody wrote about it in the newspapers, and that was exactly as it should be.
The company later gave me a small award, a framed certificate with a gold border.
But the real reward was the faces of the young engineers that morning.
I felt then that the plant was a family, not just a workplace.
They had seen that a crisis can be met with patience, listening, and a good neighbour.
Several of them went on to lead plants of their own, and they still send me greetings.
I am also very proud of my sons, who became a doctor and a software engineer through their own effort.
Lakshmi and I gave them time and books, and they did the rest.
Still, the pump night stays in my memory as the finest hour of my working life.
It combined everything I loved, which was careful listening, shared work, and a machine brought back to health.
I do not claim any genius in it, only attention.
That is the secret of most things worth doing.
My father the schoolmaster would have understood it at once.
He once told me that pride is simply the quiet gladness of a job done properly.
I think of him whenever I remember that summer.
